unit.name: Britain: Power and the People
unit.subtitle: From Magna Carta to modern protest: how citizens have shaped the British state.

lessons.title: The Citizen and the State: A Thematic Toolkit, c1170-Present
lessons.description: Meet the seven AQA factors and the four question types that frame this 850-year thematic study.
lessons.content_html:
A Thematic Study Across 850 Years

This unit is unusual. Instead of studying one short period in depth, you will leap across nearly nine centuries, from feudalism in the 1170s to twenty-first-century campaigns for racial justice. The thread that connects everything is the relationship between the citizen and the state — how ordinary people in Britain have challenged authority, and how rulers have responded. By the end you should be able to trace patterns of protest and reform from medieval revolts through to modern social movements.

In c1170, Britain was a feudal kingdom. The king ruled by divine right, most people were unfree serfs, and there was no Parliament. By 2025, Britain is a parliamentary democracy with universal suffrage, a Human Rights Act and protest protected by law. The unit asks how that journey happened — and whose pressure forced each step.

Key Fact

AQA tests seven factors across the unit: war, religion, chance, government, communication, the economy, and ideas (especially equality, democracy and representation). The role of the individual sits alongside these as an eighth strand.

The Seven Factors — Your Spine for the Whole Course

Every protest, reform and revolt you study fits one or more of these factors. You should learn to spot them quickly, because the 16-mark essay always names one and asks you to weigh it against the others.

  • War — conflict often forces change. The English Civil War (1642–51) executed a king; the First World War accelerated women’s suffrage in 1918.
  • Religion — the Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) defended Catholicism; Quaker networks drove anti-slavery campaigning in the 1780s.
  • Chance — the Black Death (1348–49) reshaped the labour market and made the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 possible.
  • Government — royal overreach (King John, Charles I) and parliamentary repression (Pitt in the 1790s, Thatcher in the 1980s) both trigger resistance.
  • Communication — printing presses, Chartist newspapers, radio in 1926 and social media for Black Lives Matter UK have all amplified protest.
  • The economy — the 1381 poll tax, the 1815 Corn Laws and 1980s unemployment all sparked organised protest.
  • Ideas — especially equality, democracy and representation. The Levellers in 1647, the Americans in 1776 and the suffragettes after 1903 all argued from ideas.

Examiner reports warn that students who present individuals like Wilberforce, Pankhurst or Cromwell as sole causes of change lose marks. Wilberforce was the parliamentary face of an abolition movement built by Quakers, freed people like Olaudah Equiano, and a national petition campaign. Always frame individuals within the conditions that made them effective.

The Four Question Types You Will Be Marked On

Paper 2 Section A always asks the same four questions in the same order. Knowing what each rewards is half the battle.

Key Fact

The four question types: 4-mark ‘two ways similar or different’, 8-mark ‘explain the significance’, 8-mark ‘explain a development’, and 16-mark factors essay. The factors essay is worth as much as the other three combined.

The 4-mark question wants two clearly distinct points, each with specific supporting detail. Comparing methods or outcomes tends to score higher than comparing causes. The 8-mark significance question rewards students who address importance both at the time and over time — a common trap is to describe what something was, not why it mattered. The 8-mark development question asks for narrative-with-causation, not just a list of events. The 16-mark factors essay must address the named factor first, then weigh it against at least two others, drawing examples from at least two of the four parts of the course.

“Explain two ways the Peasants’ Revolt and the Pilgrimage of Grace were similar.” A top answer might say: “Both were sparked by economic grievances tied to government taxation — the poll tax in 1381 and fears of new taxes in 1536. Both ended when the king broke promises made under pressure: Richard II had ringleaders executed within weeks; Henry VIII used Bigod’s rising as an excuse to renege on the Pontefract pardon.” Two distinct points, each with specific detail.

Judgement Beats Listing

The single most common mistake on this paper is listing factors without weighing them. A student who writes “the role of individuals mattered, but so did war, religion and the economy” is just inventorying causes. The mark scheme rewards students who reach a substantiated overall judgement — for example, arguing that ideas matter most because they outlast the individuals who carried them. From lesson one, train yourself to take a position and defend it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark question, give two clearly different points with specific named examples — vague comparisons cap at 2 marks. For 8-mark significance, address importance both then and now. For the 16-mark factors essay, name the factor in your opening line, weigh it against at least two others, and reach a judgement — single-period answers cap in the lower bands. Use specialist vocabulary like ‘franchise’, ‘parliamentary supremacy’, ‘mass movement’ precisely — SPaG marks reward this.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • This is a 850-year thematic study tracing how ordinary people have challenged authority and how the British state has responded.
  • Seven AQA factors — war, religion, chance, government, communication, economy, ideas — plus the role of the individual frame every lesson.
  • Four question types are tested in Paper 2 Section A: 4-mark similar/different, 8-mark significance, 8-mark development, 16-mark factors essay. Judgement beats listing every time.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the relationship between citizen and state in Britain in c1170 was different from the relationship today.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In c1170 most people were unfree serfs tied to a lord's land, with no political voice; today every adult citizen has the legal right to vote, protest and stand for office.
• In c1170 the king ruled by divine right with no Parliament; today Parliament is sovereign and the monarchy is ceremonial.
• In c1170 the only formal challenge to royal power came from the barons and the Church; today challenge is institutionalised through elections, the courts and a free press.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point with specific detail]

Mastering: Two clearly distinct ways, each fully developed with specific evidence.
Secure: Two ways with some supporting detail.
Developing: Two simple points or one developed point.
Emerging: One simple point or vague comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the seven factors framework in studying the changing relationship between citizen and state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time: each factor (war, religion, chance, government, communication, economy, ideas) names a real driver of change in different periods, helping historians explain why protest happened when it did.
• Significance over time: tracking factors across all four parts of the course shows how the same forces (e.g. ideas of representation) reappear and evolve from 1265 to 1965.
• It enables comparative judgement: by comparing how war drove change in 1646 and 1918, students reach the level of analysis the mark scheme rewards.
• It guards against single-cause explanations, which examiner reports flag as a recurring weakness.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time, with specific examples from at least two parts of the course]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of significance both then and over time, with specific evidence from multiple periods.
Secure: Clear analysis with relevant evidence; may favour one period.
Developing: Some explanation of significance; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Description of factors with little analysis of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the development of citizen rights in Britain across the period c1170 to the present day.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1215 Magna Carta: due process for free men; legal limit on royal taxation without baronial consent — but applies only to a minority.
• 1265 Simon de Montfort's Parliament: knights and burgesses summoned alongside barons — first step towards representation.
• 1649 trial and execution of Charles I: established that a monarch can be removed by his subjects; parliamentary supremacy follows.
• 1832 Great Reform Act and beyond: gradual extension of the franchise to working men (1867, 1884) and women (1918, 1928).
• 1998 Human Rights Act: rights now enshrined in domestic law.
[8 marks — Top band rewards a narrative with explicit causation between stages, not just a list of dates]

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit links between each development and the next.
Secure: Clear chronology with some causal links.
Developing: Series of events with limited links.
Emerging: Disconnected list of dates or events.

practice_questions.text: 'Ideas have been the main factor in changing the relationship between citizen and state in Britain.' Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arguments for ideas as main factor: Lockean natural rights driving 1689 Bill of Rights and 1776 American Revolution; Leveller demand for manhood suffrage at Putney 1647; suffragette slogan 'Deeds not words' built on belief in equality.
• Arguments for the role of the individual: Simon de Montfort, Wilberforce, Pankhurst, Doreen Lawrence — but examiner reports warn against treating individuals as sole causes.
• Arguments for war: English Civil War; First World War accelerating 1918 franchise; Second World War shaping the welfare state.
• Arguments for the economy: 1381 poll tax; 1815 Corn Laws; 1926 mining wages; 1981 unemployment driving Brixton.
• Judgement: ideas may be primary because they outlive their carriers, but they only translate into reform when economic and political conditions allow.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Top band rewards a sustained argument addressing the named factor and weighing it against at least two others, with examples from at least two parts of the course]

Mastering: Sustained, substantiated argument addressing the named factor and weighing against at least two others, drawing on multiple periods.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant comparison; may underweight one factor.
Developing: Some argument with basic comparison; explanation limited.
Emerging: Single-factor or single-period response.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the role of individuals and the role of ideas have been similar in driving change in Britain.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both have produced lasting reform only when conditions allowed: Wilberforce's parliamentary campaigns succeeded because Quaker networks and abolitionist petitions had built public pressure; Lockean ideas reshaped politics because the Civil War had already broken royal absolutism.
• Both can be misread as sole causes: examiner reports warn that crediting one individual or one idea ignores the war, religion or economic context that made change possible.
• Both reappear across the course: individuals (Montfort, Cromwell, Pankhurst, Lawrence) and ideas (representation, equality, rights) recur in every period, allowing comparative judgement.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, fully developed.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of judgement, rather than listing, in answering the 16-mark factors essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time of writing: the mark scheme rewards a substantiated overall judgement, not coverage of every factor — listing caps in the middle band.
• Significance over time in students' performance: examiner reports across multiple series flag inventory-style answers as the most common reason able candidates miss the top band.
• It models historical thinking: real historians weigh causes against each other, they do not just list them — students who do this are practising a transferable skill.
• Without judgement, comparison is impossible: a student cannot say a factor is 'more important' without first taking a position.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both for individual answers and for the discipline more broadly]

Mastering: Sustained analysis of why judgement matters, with specific evidence.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; evidence limited.
Emerging: Description without analysis.

lessons.title: Magna Carta and the Limits of Kingship, 1215
lessons.description: Why barons rebelled against King John, what Magna Carta said in 1215, and the gap between the.
lessons.content_html:
King John and the Road to Runnymede

By 1215, King John of England was loathed. He had inherited a strong throne from his brother Richard the Lionheart in 1199, but had managed to lose the duchy of Normandy to the French king Philip II by 1204, taking Anjou and most of his French inheritance with it. To pay for failed campaigns to recover those lands, John squeezed the barons with scutage — a payment in lieu of military service — at unprecedented rates. He demanded eleven scutages in seventeen years; his predecessors had averaged one every three years.

Religion made things worse. John quarrelled with Pope Innocent III over the appointment of Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury. The Pope put England under an interdict from 1208 to 1213, suspending most church services. John eventually surrendered, accepting England as a papal fief in 1213 to pull Innocent onto his side. The financial concession to Rome did not impress the barons.

Key Fact

King John's failures stacked up: lost Normandy and Anjou by 1204, taxed barons heavily through scutage, quarrelled with Pope Innocent III, and was decisively defeated by France at the Battle of Bouvines in July 1214. Bouvines triggered the baronial revolt that produced Magna Carta.

The Baronial Revolt and Stephen Langton

After Bouvines, the rebel barons — mostly drawn from the north and east of England — demanded that John confirm the rights they had held under earlier kings. Archbishop Langton played the crucial mediating role. He had read the coronation charter of Henry I (1100), which limited royal powers, and used it as a template. Langton was a Pope’s appointee who became a barons’ ally — a reminder that the role of the individual depends entirely on the conditions around it.

In May 1215, the rebels captured London. John was forced to negotiate at Runnymede, a meadow on the Thames between Windsor and Staines. On 15 June 1215, he sealed the document we now call Magna Carta, the ‘Great Charter’, with 63 clauses.

What Magna Carta Actually Said

Most of the 63 clauses were technical baronial grievances — rules about feudal inheritance fees, widows’ remarriage, and the misuse of royal forests. But three sections mattered for the long term:

  • The Church was guaranteed its freedoms, including freedom from royal interference in elections.
  • No scutage or aid could be raised ‘without the common counsel of the realm’ — a council of barons.
  • Clause 39 promised that ‘no free man shall be seized or imprisoned… except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.’ This is the seed of due process.

Standards of weights and measures were also regulated — an early sign that the king answered to commercial interests, not just barons. Crucially, ‘free men’ in 1215 did not mean ordinary subjects. Most of the population were unfree villeins; they had no protection from clause 39.

Examiner reports flag this repeatedly: students claim Magna Carta ‘started democracy’. It did not. It was a peace treaty between the king and a small armed group of barons, drafted to protect the elite — nobles, the Church and the City of London. The famous ‘free man’ clauses applied to roughly 10–20% of the population at most. The democratic legacy — rule of law, no taxation without representation — was constructed by lawyers and politicians centuries later, particularly in the seventeenth century.

Short-Term Failure

Within ten weeks Magna Carta was a dead letter. John wrote to Innocent III, who annulled the charter on 24 August 1215, calling it ‘shameful, demeaning, illegal and unjust’. Civil war resumed. The barons invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne. John died of dysentery in October 1216, leaving the crown to his nine-year-old son Henry III.

Long-Term Survival — The Reissues

Magna Carta survived because Henry III’s regents reissued it in 1216 and 1217 to win loyal support, and Henry confirmed it again in 1225 in return for a tax. By 1297 it was on the statute roll under Edward I. Each reissue stripped some clauses and confirmed others. The 1297 version remains technically in force today — clause 39 is still UK law.

In the 1620s, parliamentary lawyers like Sir Edward Coke held up Magna Carta against Charles I as proof that the king was under the law. Coke argued clause 39 protected every Englishman, not just ‘free men’. This re-reading shaped the 1628 Petition of Right and ultimately the trial of Charles I in 1649. The medieval document became the foundation myth of English liberty — a meaning later than the document itself.

Key Fact

Clause 39 promised no free man could be imprisoned except by lawful judgement. In 1215 it protected the elite; by 1628 lawyers used it to limit Charles I; today it is the basis of due process and habeas corpus in UK law. Its significance grew over time, not at the time.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark significance question on Magna Carta, you must address importance both at the time (limited — annulled within ten weeks, applied only to free men) and over time (became the legal foundation for parliamentary supremacy, due process and habeas corpus). Avoid the trap of writing about the modern myth as if it was true in 1215. Use specialist vocabulary like ‘scutage’, ‘feudal’, ‘clause 39’, ‘due process’ precisely.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • King John lost Normandy, taxed heavily, fought the Pope and was crushed at Bouvines in 1214 — baronial revolt followed.
  • Magna Carta in June 1215 protected the Church, limited royal taxation without consent, and promised due process for free men — not for most of the population.
  • The charter was annulled within ten weeks but reissued under Henry III. Its long-term significance was constructed by 17th-century lawyers, who turned it into a foundation of English liberty.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Magna Carta in the changing relationship between citizen and state in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Significance at the time (limited): a peace treaty between King John and rebel barons; protected the elite, not ordinary subjects; annulled by Pope Innocent III within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
• Significance at the time (real but small): clause 12 required common counsel for taxation; clause 39 promised due process for 'free men'; established that the king could be made to negotiate.
• Significance over time: reissued under Henry III in 1216, 1217, 1225 — survived as a constitutional document.
• Significance over time: 17th-century lawyers like Sir Edward Coke reinterpreted clause 39 against Charles I; foundation for the 1628 Petition of Right and parliamentary supremacy.
• Long-term legacy: clause 39 still in UK law today; basis of due process and habeas corpus; cited in the US Constitution and modern human rights debates.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time]

practice_questions.text: Explain the development of constraints on royal power between 1199 (King John's accession) and 1215 (Magna Carta).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1199–1204: John inherits a strong throne from Richard but loses Normandy and Anjou to Philip II of France.
• 1205–1213: John quarrels with Pope Innocent III; England placed under interdict 1208; John concedes 1213.
• 1213–1214: heavy scutage and arbitrary justice deepen baronial resentment; defeat at Bouvines in July 1214 strips John of military prestige.
• 1215: rebel barons capture London May 1215; Stephen Langton mediates, drawing on Henry I's coronation charter; Runnymede 15 June 1215; Magna Carta sealed.
• Each event builds the next: military failure → financial demands → political revolt.
[8 marks — Top band rewards explicit causation between stages, not a chronological list]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the limits placed on King John in 1215 were similar to the limits later placed on Charles I in the 1640s.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both limits emerged from armed revolt, not voluntary concession: barons forced John to seal Magna Carta; Parliament fought a Civil War against Charles I.
• Both centred on taxation: clause 12 of Magna Carta required common counsel for scutage; the Civil War was triggered partly by Charles's ship money and personal rule.
• Both used the language of established law against the king: Langton invoked Henry I's charter; Coke and parliamentarians invoked Magna Carta itself.
• Both produced documents claiming to bind future kings: Magna Carta (reissued repeatedly); the Petition of Right 1628 and 1689 Bill of Rights.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, fully developed.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: 'The role of individuals was the main factor in producing Magna Carta.' Evaluate the claim that this is correct
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Arguments for individuals: Stephen Langton drafted the terms using Henry I's charter as a template; King John's personal failures (Bouvines, the interdict) created the crisis; rebel barons led by Robert Fitzwalter organised the revolt.
• Arguments against — war: defeat at Bouvines 1214 stripped John of military prestige and made revolt possible.
• Arguments against — the economy: eleven scutages in seventeen years and arbitrary fines drove baronial anger.
• Arguments against — religion: papal interdict 1208–1213 weakened John; Langton's mediation flowed from his church position.
• Arguments against — government overreach: arbitrary justice, abuse of forest law, exploitation of feudal incidents.
• Cross-period weighing: ideas (rule of law) shaped 1689 and 1832 too — but only because individuals like Coke later reinterpreted Magna Carta.
• Judgement: individuals mattered, but only because military defeat, taxation crisis and church conflict had already created the conditions.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Top band rewards a sustained argument addressing the named factor and weighing it against at least two others]

Mastering: Substantiated argument addressing individuals and weighing against at least two other factors, with examples from at least two periods.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant comparison.
Developing: Some argument with basic comparison.
Emerging: Single-factor or single-period response.

Students may include:

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of clause 39 of Magna Carta.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:

• Significance over time: cited by Sir Edward Coke against Charles I in the 1620s; foundation of habeas corpus.
• Significance over time: text echoed in the 1628 Petition of Right, the US Fifth Amendment, the European Convention on Human Rights.
• Significance over time: clause 39 is still in force in UK statute today, the only medieval text on the modern statute book.
[8 marks — Top band rewards address of importance both at the time and over time]

lessons.title: Simon de Montfort and the Birth of Parliament, 1258-1265
lessons.description: How Henry III's quarrel with his barons accidentally produced the first Parliament with elected.
lessons.content_html:
Henry III and the Sicilian Business

Magna Carta was supposed to settle the question of royal power. By the 1250s, it was settling nothing. Henry III, son of King John, had reigned since 1216 and inherited his father’s habit of overreaching. His most damaging mistake was the ‘Sicilian Business’ — in 1254 he agreed with the Pope that his second son Edmund would become king of Sicily, a kingdom Henry would have to conquer first. Henry promised to fund a vast military campaign, then asked his barons to pay for it.

The barons refused. They were already angry that Henry surrounded himself with foreign favourites, especially his French half-brothers from Poitou, who held lucrative offices and lands. They had watched Henry’s government fail to enforce justice locally and ignore the spirit of Magna Carta. The Sicilian Business was the breaking point.

Key Fact

The 1254 Sicilian Business committed Henry III to conquer Sicily for his son Edmund and pay vast sums to the Pope. The barons saw it as a foreign vanity project funded from English pockets, and refused to pay. This refusal, combined with hatred of foreign favourites, broke the relationship between Henry and his nobility.

The Provisions of Oxford, 1258

In April 1258, seven barons stormed into Westminster armed and demanded reform. At a parliament in Oxford that June, they forced Henry to accept the Provisions of Oxford, sometimes called England’s first written constitution. Under the Provisions, a 15-member council of barons supervised the king. A parliament would meet three times a year. Royal sheriffs would answer to local communities, not just to the king.

The most prominent reformer was Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester. Born in France around 1208, he had married Henry’s sister Eleanor in 1238 and built a power base in the English Midlands. De Montfort was charismatic, ruthless, and committed to legal reform. He was also — ironically, given the foreign-favourites complaint — himself a Frenchman by birth.

Civil War and the Battle of Lewes, 1264

Henry chafed under the Provisions. In 1261 he asked the Pope to release him from his oath, and reasserted royal authority. The barons split. By 1263 the country was in open civil war, the Second Barons’ War. At the Battle of Lewes in May 1264, de Montfort decisively defeated the royal army and captured both King Henry III and his son Prince Edward. For the next fifteen months, de Montfort effectively ruled England.

The Parliament of January 1265

De Montfort needed broad support against royalist holdouts. In January 1265, he summoned the most innovative parliament England had ever seen. Alongside the usual barons and bishops, he called two knights from every shire and two burgesses from each major town. For the first time, commoners — townspeople and lesser landholders — sat in a national assembly.

Key Fact

The 1265 Parliament was the first to include knights of the shire and burgesses from towns alongside the barons and bishops. De Montfort summoned them not from democratic principle but because he needed political support. The accidental precedent reshaped the future Parliament permanently.

De Montfort is sometimes called the ‘father of the House of Commons’, but he was no democrat. He summoned commoners because he needed their political and military support against royalist barons who had not joined his side. The knights and burgesses he called were elite property-owners, not ordinary subjects. Voting and serving were restricted to the wealthy. The democratic significance is real but indirect — the precedent of including commoners survived; the wider franchise took 600 more years.

The Battle of Evesham, 1265

Prince Edward escaped from house arrest in May 1265 and rallied royalist forces. On 4 August 1265, at Evesham in Worcestershire, Edward’s army caught de Montfort’s smaller force. The earl was killed; his body was mutilated — head, hands, feet and genitals cut off — in a deliberate humiliation. The reform movement collapsed; Henry III was restored to full power; many of de Montfort’s lands were confiscated.

The Long-Term Impact

In the short term, the reform movement failed. But Edward I, when he became king in 1272, kept what worked. His ‘Model Parliament’ of 1295 included two knights from every shire and two burgesses from every borough — exactly de Montfort’s 1265 format. The two-chamber Parliament we know today, with House of Lords and House of Commons, evolved from these summonses. By the fourteenth century, the practice had hardened into custom.

Magna Carta in 1215 established that the king must take counsel before raising taxes. The Provisions of Oxford in 1258 turned that into a permanent supervisory council. The 1265 Parliament expanded who counted as ‘the realm’ whose counsel mattered. Each step came from baronial revolt against royal overreach — not from a deliberate plan to build democracy. The institutions were built accidentally, by men solving immediate political problems.

Each step caused the next; do not just list events. Avoid the trap of saying de Montfort ‘founded democracy’ — the mark scheme rewards precision about his power-political motives.

Key Takeaways

  • Henry III's foreign favourites and the 1254 Sicilian Business broke trust with the barons; the 1258 Provisions of Oxford forced a 15-member supervisory council on the king.
  • Simon de Montfort defeated Henry at Lewes in 1264 and ruled in his name; in January 1265 he summoned the first Parliament to include knights of the shire and burgesses.
  • De Montfort died at Evesham in August 1265, but Edward I's Model Parliament in 1295 kept the two-knights-and-two-burgesses formula — building the foundations of the modern Commons.

lessons.title: The Peasants' Revolt, 1381
lessons.description: How a poll tax, plague-era labour shortages and a young king's broken promises sparked England's.
lessons.content_html:
Long-Term Causes — The Black Death and Its Aftermath

The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 did not begin in 1381. Its causes ran back thirty years to the Black Death of 1348–49. The plague killed roughly 40% of the English population in eighteen months. Whole villages were abandoned. The labour shortage that followed gave surviving peasants real bargaining power for the first time. Lords had to compete for workers; wages climbed; some peasants left their manor without permission, hoping a new lord would not ask awkward questions.

Parliament responded with the Statute of Labourers in 1351. The law tried to freeze wages at pre-plague levels, ban peasants from leaving their manor, and force the unemployed to accept work for whoever offered it first. Enforcement was patchy — lords who needed labour quietly paid higher wages anyway — but the statute symbolised a regime that protected lords from the consequences of a labour market changing in workers’ favour.

Key Fact

The Black Death of 1348–49 killed about 40% of the English population, creating a labour shortage that gave peasants real wage-bargaining power. The 1351 Statute of Labourers tried to suppress this shift by freezing wages at pre-plague levels — a long-term grievance that fed into the 1381 revolt.

Mid-Term Causes — War, Boy Kings and a Hated Regime

The Hundred Years War with France was going badly. English forces had lost the territory that Edward III won at Crécy and Poitiers, and the war was draining the treasury. Edward III died in 1377; his successor was the ten-year-old Richard II. Real power lay with the king’s uncle John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster — widely loathed for his corruption and connections to a war that produced taxes but no victories.

Religion mattered too. The radical preacher John Ball roamed Kent and Essex preaching social equality. His most famous line summed up the mood: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?” God had not created lords and peasants — humans had. That argument, repeated in village churches and at market crosses, gave revolt a religious legitimacy.

The Trigger — The 1381 Poll Tax

A poll tax is a flat tax charged per head. England had three of them in four years. The first in 1377 cost 4d per adult; the second in 1379 was graduated by income; the third in 1381 was a flat 12d — three days’ wages for a labourer — on every adult over fifteen. Evasion was rampant; tax collectors used aggressive methods to extract payment, including, according to one chronicler, lifting peasant girls’ skirts to check whether they were old enough to be taxed.

In late May 1381, villagers in Fobbing, Essex, drove off the tax collectors with sticks. The rising spread fast. Within ten days, peasants from Essex and Kent were marching on London under the banner of Wat Tyler, an obscure but charismatic figure who had served as a soldier in France.

Key Fact

The rebels demanded an end to serfdom, the abolition of the poll tax, the death of ‘traitors’ like John of Gaunt, the dissolution of corrupt landlordism, and a new relationship between the king and his people. Their grievances combined economic hardship, religious idealism and political resentment.

The Rising in London, June 1381

On 13 June, Tyler’s men crossed London Bridge into the city. They burned the Savoy Palace, John of Gaunt’s opulent residence on the Strand, smashing its treasures rather than looting them. They opened prisons, killing Flemish merchants in Cheapside, and stormed the Tower of London — dragging out and beheading the Archbishop of Canterbury Simon Sudbury (also Lord Chancellor) and the Treasurer Robert Hales. Their heads were paraded on London Bridge.

On 14 June, the fourteen-year-old Richard II rode out to meet the rebels at Mile End. He listened to their grievances and granted charters abolishing serfdom and offering pardons. Many rebels left for home, believing they had won.

Smithfield and the King’s Trick

The next day, 15 June, Richard met Tyler again at Smithfield. The encounter ended in violence — the Mayor of London, William Walworth, struck Tyler with a dagger; Tyler fell from his horse and was killed. The rebels were on the brink of attacking when the boy-king rode forward and shouted, according to chronicler Jean Froissart, “You shall have no captain but me.” The rebels, perhaps stunned, dispersed.

Within weeks Richard had revoked the charters. “Villeins ye are still, and villeins ye shall remain,” he reportedly told a delegation. Ringleaders were hunted down; John Ball was hanged, drawn and quartered at St Albans on 15 July 1381. Around 150 rebels were executed in total. The king’s broken promise echoes the pattern that will recur with the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1537 and the Peterloo crowds in 1819 — rulers buy time with concessions, then renege when the moment passes.

Impact — What the Revolt Achieved

In the immediate term, the revolt failed: leaders died, charters were revoked, the rebels lost. But the poll tax was abandoned and not levied again for centuries. Serfdom continued to decline organically over the next century, partly because lords feared another rising. And a powerful precedent was set — ordinary people had marched on London, killed the Archbishop of Canterbury and forced the king to negotiate face-to-face. After 1381, no English regime could ignore the political existence of commoners.

Several AQA factors converge. Chance: the Black Death created the labour shortage that empowered peasants. The economy: the poll tax was the immediate trigger. Communication: travelling preachers like John Ball spread ideas through sermons and at market crosses. The role of the individual: Wat Tyler and John Ball gave the rising leadership and ideology. Government: a weak boy-king regime under John of Gaunt’s unpopular guidance was the ultimate target. No single factor ‘caused’ 1381 — the conjunction did.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark factors essay on whether the role of the individual caused the Peasants’ Revolt, the named factor must come first — Tyler and Ball gave the rising leadership and a slogan. Then weigh against the economy (poll tax, post-plague wages), chance (Black Death), and government (boy king, John of Gaunt’s unpopularity). Reach a judgement: individuals shaped HOW the revolt happened, but the underlying conditions made revolt likely with or without them. Avoid ‘then this happened’ chronology — show causation between factors.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Long-term causes: the Black Death (1348–49) killed 40% of the population; the 1351 Statute of Labourers tried to suppress the resulting wage rises.
  • The 1381 poll tax of 12d per adult was the trigger; rebels under Wat Tyler and the preacher John Ball marched on London, burned the Savoy Palace and beheaded the Archbishop of Canterbury.
  • Richard II's promises at Mile End were revoked within weeks; ringleaders were executed but the poll tax was dropped and serfdom slowly declined — a failed rising with lasting consequences.

lessons.title: The Pilgrimage of Grace, 1536
lessons.description: The largest peacetime revolt in English history and the religious crisis behind 30,000 marchers.
lessons.content_html:
The Religious Earthquake of the 1530s

In the early 1530s Henry VIII broke with Rome to secure a divorce from Catherine of Aragon. The 1534 Act of Supremacy declared the king Supreme Head of the Church of England. From 1535 his chief minister Thomas Cromwell sent commissioners around the country to value Church property. By 1536 the smaller monasteries — those with incomes under £200 a year — were being closed in the Dissolution of the Monasteries, their lands sold to the Crown and its supporters. To many ordinary northerners this looked less like reform and more like a war on the religion their families had practised for centuries.

Why the North Rose: Four Causes Tangled Together

The Pilgrimage of Grace had no single cause. Religious grievance was the loudest: monasteries were not just spiritual centres but the social and economic heart of northern villages, providing schools, almshouses, hospitality and employment. The dissolution threatened to destroy a whole local infrastructure. But the rising also drew on economic anxiety — rumours that Henry would tax baptisms, marriages and burials, on top of bad harvests in 1535 and 1536 that pushed grain prices up. Politically, northerners resented the ‘low-born’ advisers around the king — Cromwell above all, who they saw as displacing the traditional nobility. Socially, peasant tenants and town gentry alike were uneasy about rising rents and enclosure on monastic lands now in lay hands.

Key Fact

The Pilgrimage of Grace combined religious, economic, political and social grievances. Religion was loudest — the dissolution of smaller monasteries from 1536 felt like an attack on Catholic identity — but rumours of new taxes, hostility to Cromwell, and rising rents all fed in. No single cause explains the scale of 30,000 men in the field.

The Lincolnshire Rising and the March of 30,000

The trouble began at Louth in Lincolnshire on 1 October 1536, when a Cromwell commissioner arrived to dissolve the local monastery. Within a week 40,000 men were assembled. Henry sent the Duke of Suffolk with a small royal force and a public pardon; the Lincolnshire rising collapsed by mid-October. But it had already lit a longer fuse across the Pennines.

In Yorkshire a Yorkshire lawyer named Robert Aske took command of what he called the Pilgrimage of Grace — a deliberately religious word, presenting the rising as a holy procession rather than a rebellion. Around 30,000 marchers, well organised and heavily armed, gathered under the banner of the Five Wounds of Christ. They took York, Pontefract and Hull. They drafted articles demanding the restoration of the monasteries, the removal of Cromwell, the protection of the Catholic Church and a free Parliament held in the north.

Aske chose the word carefully. Calling the movement a ‘pilgrimage’ framed it as a religious act rather than a treasonous rebellion against the king. The marchers wore badges of the Five Wounds of Christ and sang hymns as they advanced. Aske claimed the rebels had no quarrel with Henry himself — only with his evil advisers. This framing was politically useful. It allowed gentry and even some clergy to join without admitting open treason, and it put pressure on Henry to listen rather than fight.

Henry's Trap: Pardon, then Reprisal

Henry could not match 30,000 northerners in the field. He had perhaps 8,000 men under the Duke of Norfolk and could not raise more without delay. So Norfolk played for time. At Doncaster in early December 1536 he negotiated. He offered a free pardon, promised that grievances would be discussed in a Parliament held at York, and gave assurances that the monasteries would be reviewed. Aske, trusting the king's word, ordered the marchers home for Christmas.

The promises were never going to hold. In January 1537 a smaller separate rising led by Sir Francis Bigod broke out in the East Riding without Aske's authority. Henry seized the excuse. Bigod's revolt, he argued, proved the northerners could not be trusted. Pardons were withdrawn, martial law was imposed, and around 200 ringleaders were executed across the north. Robert Aske was tricked into returning to London, where Henry feasted him at court before having him arrested, transported back to York and hanged in chains from the city walls in July 1537.

Key Fact

Henry VIII used a free pardon and the promise of a northern Parliament to make the marchers go home. Within months, on the pretext of a smaller follow-up rising, around 200 ringleaders were executed and Aske was hanged at York in July 1537. The pattern of broken royal promise repeats Richard II's revocation of the 1381 charters.

Impact: The North Silenced, the Reformation Continued

In the short term the rising failed: Aske and the leaders were dead, the dissolution accelerated through the larger monasteries between 1538 and 1540, and a Council of the North was strengthened to keep the region under direct royal control. But the Pilgrimage was the largest peacetime rising in English history, and its scale shocked the Tudor regime into a permanent watchfulness over the north. Later northern risings (the Prayer Book Rebellion of 1549, the Northern Earls of 1569) framed themselves more cautiously and were crushed faster. Royal authority emerged stronger, but its limits had been exposed: a religious cause could move tens of thousands.

The shape of the Pilgrimage echoes the Peasants' Revolt 155 years earlier. Both were touched off by a specific grievance — the poll tax in 1381, the dissolution in 1536. Both produced large-scale risings led by named individuals (Tyler and Ball; Aske). Both involved a face-to-face negotiation in which the Crown bought time with promises. Both ended with those promises broken and the ringleaders executed. The lesson AQA wants you to draw is that royal authority in the medieval and early modern periods was often performative — the king bargained when he had to, then punished when he could.

The Factor Thread

This lesson is dominated by religion — the dissolution of the monasteries and Catholic identity in the north. But several other factors converge. The economy: rumours of new taxes and bad harvests; government: Cromwell's aggressive style of central administration; the role of the individual: Aske's choice of pilgrimage framing and Henry's choice of betrayal. Religion will return as a driver in the seventeenth century when the New Model Army's Puritan radicals push for reform; the role of the individual repeats with Cromwell, the Pankhursts and Doreen Lawrence.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark ‘two ways the Pilgrimage of Grace was similar to the Peasants' Revolt’ question, pick the comparisons most students miss: both involved royal promises that were broken, both ended with the leaders executed despite earlier pardons. Avoid surface similarities (‘both were protests’) — examiners reward genuinely distinct points. Each comparison needs specific support: name Aske and Tyler, name 1537 and 1381.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) was the largest peacetime rising in English history; around 30,000 marched under the banner of the Five Wounds of Christ against Henry VIII's break with Rome and the dissolution of the smaller monasteries.
  • Causes were tangled: religion was loudest, but rumours of new taxes, hostility to Cromwell, rising rents and northern political resentment all fed in.
  • Robert Aske trusted Henry's pardon; Bigod's smaller follow-up rising in 1537 gave Henry the excuse to renege. Around 200 ringleaders were executed; Aske was hanged in chains at York. The pattern of pardon-then-betrayal echoes Richard II in 1381.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) was similar to the Peasants' Revolt (1381).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both involved face-to-face negotiations between the rebels and royal representatives, with the Crown offering pardons and promises — Richard II at Mile End in 1381, the Duke of Norfolk at Doncaster in 1536.
• Both ended in betrayal: Richard II revoked the charters within weeks; Henry VIII used Bigod's 1537 rising as an excuse to renege on the Doncaster pardon and execute around 200 ringleaders.
• Both were led by named individuals whose execution became a symbol — John Ball hanged July 1381, Robert Aske hanged in chains at York July 1537.
• Both drew religious legitimacy from sacred imagery — Ball's preaching from Genesis; the Five Wounds of Christ banner of 1536.

[4 marks — 2 marks per similarity: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed comparison with example]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, each with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points or one developed point.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Pilgrimage of Grace in the changing relationship between the citizen and the state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: largest peacetime rising in English history; around 30,000 under arms forced Henry VIII into negotiation he could not afford militarily.
• At the time: exposed the limits of Tudor royal authority — Henry had no army to match the marchers and had to play for time with the Doncaster pardon.
• At the time: led to swift reprisals — around 200 executions, Aske hanged at York 1537, dissolution accelerated through the larger monasteries 1538-40.
• Over time: strengthened the Council of the North as a permanent instrument of royal control over the region.
• Over time: shaped how later northern risings (Prayer Book 1549, Northern Earls 1569) framed themselves and how quickly they were crushed.
• Over time: a powerful precedent that religion could move tens of thousands — revisited under the Stuarts and in the Civil War era.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise dates and a clear judgement on what changed.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the rising without explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain the development of popular protest against royal authority between 1381 and 1536.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1381 Peasants' Revolt: peasants and lower clergy march on London; demands centred on serfdom and the poll tax; royal promises at Mile End revoked within weeks.
• Religious legitimacy entered the language of revolt — John Ball's preaching from Genesis foreshadowed the Five Wounds banner of 1536.
• 1450 Cade's Revolt (optional context): Kentish rising blamed Henry VI's corrupt advisers; pattern of attacking ‘evil counsellors’ rather than the king.
• 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace: 30,000 rise under religious banners; demands centred on monasteries and royal advisers; cross-class coalition of peasants, gentry and clergy.
• Continuity: the Crown bargains when outnumbered, then reneges and executes the leaders — Tyler and Ball, Aske and the Doncaster ringleaders.
• Change: the social base broadens. 1381 was peasant-led; 1536 included gentry and clergy. Religion replaces feudal grievance as the primary frame.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal explanation linking each phase to the next with precise detail across the period.
Secure: Clear explanation of the main developments with examples.
Developing: Some development, but events listed rather than linked.
Emerging: A few events identified without clear development.

practice_questions.text: ‘Religion was the main factor in causing popular uprisings against royal authority in the medieval and early modern periods.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh religion against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course.

In support of religion as the main factor:
• 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace: dissolution of the monasteries, Five Wounds of Christ banner, demands for restoration of Catholic worship; 30,000 marchers.
• 1381 Peasants' Revolt: John Ball's preaching from Genesis (‘When Adam delved and Eve span...’) gave the rising religious legitimacy.
• Later: 1640s Civil War — Puritan radicals in the New Model Army drove constitutional change.

Weighed against the economy:
• 1381 trigger was the 1381 poll tax of 12d per adult, building on the long-term Statute of Labourers grievance.
• 1536: rumours of new taxes on baptisms, burials and marriages, plus bad harvests, fed alongside religious anger.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Aske's choice to frame the 1536 rising as a pilgrimage was decisive; without it the gentry might not have joined.
• Tyler and Ball gave the 1381 revolt leadership; Cromwell and Henry shaped the response in 1536.

Weighed against government:
• A weak boy-king regime in 1381 (Richard II under John of Gaunt) and Henry VIII's reliance on Cromwell's centralised administration in the 1530s both created political vulnerabilities.

Judgement: Top answers argue religion was the primary frame in 1536 and an important driver in 1381, but in both cases economic grievance, government weakness and individual leadership combined to make the rising large enough to matter. Religion shaped how revolt was justified; the economy made it likely.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing religion against at least two other factors with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them.
Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Robert Aske in the Pilgrimage of Grace.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: as a Yorkshire lawyer he gave the rising legitimacy and discipline; coordinated the capture of York, Pontefract and Hull and drafted the rebels' articles.
• At the time: his choice to frame the movement as a ‘pilgrimage’ under the Five Wounds banner allowed gentry and clergy to join without open treason.
• At the time: his trust in Henry's pardon at Doncaster (December 1536) demobilised the marchers and exposed him to betrayal.
• Over time: his execution at York in 1537 became a Catholic memory of Tudor faithlessness, used during the Northern Earls' rising of 1569.
• Over time: the example of Aske showed later opposition movements that royal pardons could not be trusted — an attitude visible in seventeenth-century parliamentarians.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of who Aske was without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the actions of Henry VIII's government in 1536-37 were different from the actions of Richard II's government in 1381.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: Henry VIII's reprisals were more systematic — around 200 executions across the north under martial law in 1537, compared with around 150 in 1381 and largely concentrated on identified ringleaders.
• Difference: Henry used a manufactured excuse (Bigod's 1537 follow-up rising) to renege on the Doncaster pardon, where Richard II simply revoked the charters by royal will.
• Difference: Henry strengthened the Council of the North as a permanent instrument of control; Richard II made no comparable institutional change in 1381.
• Difference: Cromwell's role as a ‘low-born’ chief minister was a target of the rebels themselves in 1536, where the 1381 rebels targeted John of Gaunt as the king's uncle — a difference in the social politics of unpopular advisers.

[4 marks — 2 marks per difference: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed comparison with example]

Mastering: Two distinct differences, each with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two differences with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

lessons.title: The English Revolution: Civil War, Regicide and Republic, 1642-1660
lessons.description: How a quarrel over money and religion ended with a king on the scaffold and England as a republic.
lessons.content_html:
A King Who Believed He Answered Only to God

Charles I came to the throne in 1625 holding firmly to the doctrine of the Divine Right of Kings. He saw Parliament not as a partner in government but as a body that occasionally voted him money. From 1629 he ruled without Parliament for eleven years — the ‘Personal Rule’ — raising revenue through unpopular schemes like ship money, a tax originally imposed only on coastal towns but extended inland. Religious changes under Archbishop William Laud brought ceremony, altar rails and bishops' authority back into English worship, alarming Puritans who saw it as a slide back to Catholicism.

The Slide to War, 1640-42

The Personal Rule collapsed when Scottish Covenanters, resisting Laud's prayer book, invaded northern England. Charles needed money for an army, and only Parliament could vote it. The Long Parliament that met in November 1640 attacked the king's ministers (Strafford executed 1641), abolished the prerogative courts, and in December 1641 issued the Grand Remonstrance — a list of over 200 grievances. In January 1642 Charles tried to arrest five MPs in the Commons chamber, including John Pym. He failed; the Speaker refused to give them up. Within months both sides were raising armies. The First Civil War (1642-46) had begun.

Key Fact

The English Revolution had four interlocking causes. Ideas: Charles I's belief in Divine Right vs Parliament's claim to consent. Religion: Laudian reforms vs Puritan reformers. Money: ship money and the Personal Rule (1629-40). Political crisis: the Grand Remonstrance and the failed arrest of the Five Members in January 1642.

The New Model Army and the Politics of the Camp

In 1645 Parliament reorganised its forces into the New Model Army — full-time, paid, disciplined, and recruited and promoted by merit rather than aristocratic connection. Sir Thomas Fairfax was its commander; Oliver Cromwell its lieutenant-general of horse. At Naseby in June 1645 the New Model Army crushed Charles's main field army. The First Civil War effectively ended in 1646 with Charles's surrender.

But the army was now a political force. Soldiers had risked their lives for Parliament and were owed back pay. Many were Puritans with strong religious convictions. From within the ranks emerged a movement called the Levellers, led by John Lilburne. Their 1647 Agreement of the People argued for manhood suffrage (excluding servants and beggars), regular elections, religious liberty and equality before the law — the most democratic programme yet seen in England.

In October 1647 senior officers and Leveller agitators met in St Mary's Church, Putney, to debate the future constitution. The exchange between Colonel Thomas Rainsborough and Henry Ireton was the most famous moment in English democratic history before the Chartists. Rainsborough argued, “The poorest he that is in England hath a life to live as the greatest he” — and therefore had a right to a vote. Ireton replied that only those with property had a real stake in the country. The debates were never resolved, but their text survived and became a touchstone of British radicalism: even Chartists in the 1830s and 40s explicitly cited Rainsborough.

Trial and Execution of a King, January 1649

Charles started a Second Civil War in 1648 from his island prison at Carisbrooke, plotting with the Scots. The army, furious, decided he could not be trusted alive. In December 1648 Colonel Pride excluded MPs who wanted to negotiate, leaving a smaller ‘Rump Parliament’ that voted to put the king on trial. The trial opened on 20 January 1649 in Westminster Hall. Charles refused to plead, denying the court's jurisdiction. He was found guilty of treason. On 30 January 1649, he was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall. The English had executed their king.

Key Fact

Charles I was tried by his own subjects under his own name in Westminster Hall and beheaded on 30 January 1649. For the first time in European history a reigning king had been publicly executed under law by a court claiming to act on the people's authority. Divine Right of Kings, in practice, was finished.

The Republic That Wasn't a Democracy

From 1649 to 1660 England was a republic — the Commonwealth and, from 1653, the Protectorate under Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector. Power did not pass to the people. Cromwell suppressed the Levellers (the 1649 Burford mutineers were shot), dissolved the Rump Parliament in 1653 and ruled with the army's backing. He turned down the offer of the crown in 1657 but lived in many ways as a king — addressed as ‘Your Highness’, choosing his successor (his son Richard).

Cromwell died in September 1658. Within two years the regime had collapsed. The Restoration of May 1660 brought Charles II back from exile. The republic was over. But Parliament was now permanently superior. Charles II reigned with Parliament's tolerance, and his brother James II was driven out in 1688 when he tried to assert royal authority again. Divine Right was never seriously claimed in England after the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89.

The misconception trap is to call the Civil War a ‘fight for democracy’. Most parliamentarians wanted a constitutional monarchy, not a republic. The Levellers were suppressed by Cromwell, and the Restoration brought back the monarchy. But the long-term significance is real: kings could be removed, Parliament was permanently superior, and a body of democratic ideas (manhood suffrage, religious liberty, equality before the law) had been articulated by the Levellers in the Agreement of the People. Chartists, suffragettes and modern democrats all traced their language back to Putney.

The Factor Thread

The English Revolution is the cleanest case study in the unit for the factor of ideas: Divine Right against parliamentary authority, Leveller democracy against Ireton's defence of property. Religion: Laudian conformity against Puritan reform. War: 1642-51 created the New Model Army that gave radical ideas an institutional vehicle. Government: Personal Rule and ship money set up the constitutional collapse. The factors converge on the scaffold of 1649 — one of the central images in this entire 850-year course.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘explain the significance of the trial and execution of Charles I’ question, you must address importance both at the time AND over time. At the time: the precedent that a king could be tried and executed by his own subjects. Over time: parliamentary supremacy was permanently established (visible in 1688 and after) and Leveller ideas seeded later reform movements. Avoid simply describing the trial — examiners reward analysis of why it mattered.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The English Revolution sprang from Charles I's belief in Divine Right, conflict with Parliament over money and religion, the Personal Rule (1629-40), and the failed arrest of the Five Members in 1642.
  • The New Model Army (1645) gave Parliament victory at Naseby and became a vehicle for political radicalism — the Levellers, the Putney Debates and the Agreement of the People.
  • The trial and execution of Charles I (January 1649) ended Divine Right in practice; the Restoration of 1660 brought back the monarchy but left Parliament permanently superior — a turning point that seeded later democratic movements.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the trial and execution of Charles I in the changing relationship between the citizen and the state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: a reigning king tried by his own subjects in Westminster Hall and beheaded on 30 January 1649 — an unprecedented act in European history.
• At the time: established the Commonwealth republic (1649-60) under Cromwell and the Rump Parliament; Divine Right could no longer be defended in practice.
• Over time: parliamentary supremacy was permanently established — Charles II returned in 1660 only on Parliament's terms, James II was driven out in 1688.
• Over time: the trial set a constitutional precedent that a head of state could be held accountable; cited by 18th-century American revolutionaries and later democratic movements.
• Over time: Leveller ideas articulated during the war (Agreement of the People, Putney Debates) became foundational to later British radicalism — explicitly cited by Chartists in the 1830s and 40s.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise dates and a clear judgement.
Secure: Clear explanation of significance with examples in both periods.
Developing: Significance weighted to one period only.
Emerging: Description of the trial without explanation of why it mattered.

practice_questions.text: Explain how political radicalism developed during the Civil War era.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1642 outbreak: Parliament fights for limits on royal power, not republicanism — most MPs want a constitutional monarchy.
• 1645 New Model Army: professional, ideological, recruiting by merit rather than aristocratic connection — creates a new political class.
• 1647 Putney Debates: Leveller agitators and senior officers debate the future constitution; Rainsborough argues for the right of ‘the poorest he’ to vote.
• 1647 Agreement of the People: Levellers publish a written constitution proposing manhood suffrage, equal constituencies and religious liberty.
• 1649 regicide and Commonwealth: a republic without democracy — Levellers suppressed at Burford May 1649, Rump Parliament dissolved 1653.
• 1653 Protectorate: Cromwell rules as Lord Protector, much like a king with Parliament's tolerance — political radicalism is contained but not extinguished.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal explanation linking each phase to the next with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation of the main developments with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development, but events listed rather than linked.
Emerging: A few events identified without clear development.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the demands of the Levellers were similar to the demands of the Chartists.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Similarity: both demanded an extension of the franchise to ordinary men — the Agreement of the People (1647) proposed manhood suffrage (excluding servants); the People's Charter (1838) demanded universal manhood suffrage.
• Similarity: both proposed equal-sized constituencies, removing the unfair advantages of small or rotten boroughs.
• Similarity: both used the printing press to organise nationally — Leveller pamphlets in the 1640s, the Northern Star in the 1840s.
• Similarity: both were rejected in their own moment but their ideas eventually became law — manhood suffrage in 1918, equal constituencies and the secret ballot earlier.

[4 marks — 2 marks per similarity: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed comparison with example]

Mastering: Two distinct similarities, each with precise detail.
Secure: Two similarities with some support.
Developing: Two simple points.
Emerging: One simple point.

practice_questions.text: ‘Ideas were the main factor in causing the English Revolution.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh ideas against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement and examples from at least two parts of the course.

In support of ideas as the main factor:
• Charles I's commitment to Divine Right made compromise with Parliament constitutionally impossible.
• Parliament's claim that taxation required consent (Petition of Right 1628, Grand Remonstrance 1641) drew on long-running constitutional ideas going back to Magna Carta.
• Once war broke out, the New Model Army incubated more radical ideas — Leveller manhood suffrage, religious liberty — that pushed events further than most parliamentarians wanted.

Weighed against religion:
• Laudian reforms threatened Puritan worship and revived fears of Catholicism — the Scottish Covenanters' 1639-40 invasion was triggered by the prayer book.
• Religion supplied the language and motivation for many New Model Army soldiers; Cromwell's Puritan faith shaped the Commonwealth.

Weighed against money:
• Ship money and the eleven-year Personal Rule (1629-40) created the constitutional crisis; only Parliament could grant lawful taxation.
• The Long Parliament was summoned because Charles needed money for the Bishops' Wars; without that need there might have been no political confrontation.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Charles I's personal inflexibility — refusing to compromise, attempting to arrest the Five Members — made constitutional crisis into civil war.
• Cromwell's personal authority shaped the Protectorate and the limits of Leveller radicalism.

Cross-period weighing:
• Compare with 1381 (economic trigger) and 1536 (religious frame) — ideas of representation are most central in 1642 of the three.
• Long-term trajectory: ideas of consent and accountability seeded by the Civil War recur in 1776 (American Revolution) and 1832 (Reform Act).

Judgement: Top answers argue ideas about Divine Right vs parliamentary authority structured the conflict, but money (ship money), religion (Laudian reforms) and Charles's personal inflexibility were all needed to convert constitutional disagreement into civil war. Ideas were the frame; the other factors supplied the heat.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from across the period and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with examples; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses several factors but does not consistently weigh them.
Emerging: Single-period or single-factor response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the New Model Army in the English Revolution.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: gave Parliament decisive military victory, especially at Naseby in June 1645 — ended the First Civil War.
• At the time: its discipline, regular pay and merit-based promotion broke the aristocratic model of military command.
• At the time: it became a political vehicle — Putney Debates 1647, the Agreement of the People, the December 1648 Pride's Purge that enabled the regicide.
• Over time: it suppressed the Levellers at Burford in 1649, showing the limits of its radicalism, but also kept Cromwell in power without Parliament — pioneering a politically powerful standing army.
• Over time: gave 19th-century radicals and Chartists a heritage of organised, principled British radicalism to draw on.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance argument covering both at the time and over time, with precise detail.
Secure: Clear significance argument with examples.

lessons.title: The American Revolution and 'No Taxation Without Representation', 1763-1783
lessons.description: How ideas born in 17th-century England exploded in America and shaped later British reform.
lessons.content_html:
A Bankrupt Empire After 1763

When the Seven Years War ended in 1763 Britain emerged victorious but exhausted. The national debt had nearly doubled. Britain now controlled an enlarged North American empire, and the army needed to defend it had to be paid for. Parliament reasoned that the colonists, having been protected from the French at British expense, should help cover the cost. The thirteen American colonies disagreed. They had no MPs at Westminster, and they argued that taxing them without their consent broke a principle that ran from Magna Carta through the Civil War — no taxation without representation.

From Stamps to Tea, 1765-1773

The first direct tax was the Stamp Act of 1765, which required printed materials in the colonies — newspapers, legal documents, even playing cards — to carry a tax stamp. The colonial response was immediate. Mobs intimidated stamp distributors, the Stamp Act Congress drafted a unified protest, and merchants boycotted British goods. Parliament repealed the act in 1766 but issued the Declaratory Act asserting its right to legislate for the colonies ‘in all cases whatsoever’.

The Townshend Duties of 1767 reignited the dispute by taxing imports including tea, glass, paint and paper. British troops were sent to Boston in 1768 to keep order; on 5 March 1770 they fired on a hostile crowd, killing five — the Boston Massacre. In December 1773, colonists disguised as Mohawks tipped 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston harbour — the Boston Tea Party. Parliament's response, the Coercive Acts of 1774, closed Boston harbour and stripped Massachusetts of self-government. The colonies began to coordinate as never before.

Key Fact

British attempts to tax the American colonies built towards revolution in steps: Stamp Act 1765, Townshend Duties 1767, Boston Massacre 1770, Boston Tea Party 1773, Coercive Acts 1774. Each step deepened the colonial argument that taxation without representation was unconstitutional.

Declaration of Independence, 1776

By April 1775 fighting had broken out at Lexington and Concord. The Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia voted on 4 July 1776 to adopt the Declaration of Independence, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson. Its language drew directly on the English political tradition. ‘All men are created equal’ and the right to ‘life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness’ were Lockean ideas already familiar in British radicalism. The argument that governments derive their power from the consent of the governed and could be replaced when they failed echoed the parliamentarians of 1649. The Declaration listed 27 grievances against George III — in effect, the case for the prosecution.

The War and the World, 1775-1783

The war was long and unwinnable for Britain. George Washington's Continental Army held together despite defeats. After the American victory at Saratoga in 1777, France entered the war in 1778, followed by Spain in 1779 and the Dutch in 1780 — turning a colonial dispute into a global conflict that stretched the Royal Navy thin. The decisive defeat came at Yorktown in October 1781, where Lord Cornwallis surrendered an army of 7,000 to a combined American-French force. Britain accepted independence in the Treaty of Paris in September 1783.

Britain had a smaller population than the colonies, an over-stretched navy, and supply lines 3,000 miles long. The French alliance after 1778 was decisive: French money, French ships and French troops at Yorktown ended any realistic chance of British military victory. Politically, Lord North's government, which had pushed the Coercive Acts in 1774, fell in March 1782 once defeat became unavoidable. The loss of America discredited the ‘king's friends’ faction in Parliament and gave reformers like Christopher Wyvill an opening to revive demands for parliamentary reform at home.

The Revolution Bounces Back to Britain

The American Revolution did not just remove thirteen colonies from the British empire — it produced a working model of representative government on the other side of the Atlantic that British radicals could point to for the rest of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Christopher Wyvill's Yorkshire Association launched a petition campaign for parliamentary reform in 1779-83, explicitly drawing on the American example. John Wilkes's earlier movement for press freedom and electoral reform gained renewed energy. Tom Paine, who had moved to Philadelphia in 1774 and written the influential pamphlet Common Sense for the American cause in 1776, returned to attack the British constitution in Rights of Man (1791-92).

Key Fact

The American Revolution produced a written constitution and a republic that became a permanent reference point for British radicals. The Yorkshire Association (1779-83), John Wilkes, Thomas Paine's Rights of Man (1791-92), and later the Chartists all explicitly cited American precedent. The Revolution's slogan — no taxation without representation — became one of the founding arguments of British democratic reform.

Connecting the Pieces: 1215, 1649, 1776

The American Revolution sits at a hinge point in this thematic study. Magna Carta in 1215 established the principle that even a king was subject to law. Simon de Montfort's Parliament in 1265 introduced the principle of representation. The trial of Charles I in 1649 demonstrated that a monarch could be removed when he broke the law. The American Revolution in 1776 took the logic one step further: a Parliament that misrepresents the people could itself be removed. Each step broadened the social base of who counted as a citizen with rights against the state.

It is tempting to read the American Revolution as a popular rising like 1381 or 1536. It was not. The Patriot leadership came largely from colonial elites — merchants, lawyers, planters — who already had political voice in their local assemblies. They were defending privileges they already enjoyed against perceived British infringement. The Declaration's promise of equality was, at the time, restricted: enslaved Africans were not freed, women were not enfranchised, and Native Americans were displaced. The Revolution's significance for British history is that its principles, once written down, could not be confined to the people who wrote them — later movements (abolition, Chartism, suffragism) used those same principles to demand far more.

The Factor Thread

The American Revolution is best read as a victory of ideas — representation, consent, natural rights — combined with the economy (war debt, taxation), government (Lord North's miscalculations) and communication (pamphlets like Common Sense, the colonial postal network, transatlantic newspapers). It returns the unit to the question first raised in 1215 and 1649: where does political authority actually come from? The American answer — from the consent of the governed — reshaped British politics for the next century.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘explain the development of the idea of representation between 1215 and 1783’ question, link the stages causally rather than just listing them. Magna Carta limits royal power; the 1265 Parliament adds representation; 1649 shows kings can be removed; 1776 extends the principle to Parliament itself. Avoid ‘then this happened’ chronology — show how each step made the next thinkable.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • War debt from the Seven Years War (ended 1763) drove British taxation of the colonies; the Stamp Act 1765, Townshend Duties 1767, Boston Tea Party 1773 and Coercive Acts 1774 built towards revolution.
  • The Declaration of Independence in July 1776 used Lockean ideas already familiar in British radicalism — consent of the governed, natural rights — to justify breaking from Britain. French entry in 1778 and the surrender at Yorktown 1781 forced British recognition of independence in 1783.
  • The Revolution bounced back to shape British reform: the Yorkshire Association, Wilkes, Paine's Rights of Man and later the Chartists all drew on American precedent; ‘no taxation without representation’ became a founding argument of British democratic reform.

practice_questions.text: Explain the development of the idea of representation in Britain between 1215 and 1783.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1215 Magna Carta: established the principle that the king could not levy taxes without the consent of a council of barons; in practice this protected only an elite, but the language of consent entered English law.
• 1265 Simon de Montfort's Parliament: knights and burgesses included alongside barons and bishops — representation of commoners introduced as an emergency measure but kept by Edward I's 1295 Model Parliament.
• 1640s-1649 English Revolution: Parliament asserts that the king cannot tax or rule without it; Charles I's trial and execution in 1649 establishes that a king who breaks the law can be removed.
• 1647 Levellers' Agreement of the People: manhood suffrage proposed; rejected at the time but the language of representation deepens.
• 1776 American Revolution: colonies argue that a Parliament without their representation cannot tax them; the Declaration of Independence builds on Lockean ideas and the English Civil War tradition.
• Each stage broadens the social base — barons, then commoners, then the propertyless — and gives later British reformers a heritage to draw on.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal explanation linking each phase to the next with precise detail across the period.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development, but events listed rather than linked.
Emerging: A few events identified without clear development.
